name: Cognitive Development and Piaget
what: This subtopic covers cognitive development as a lifelong process underpinned by biological maturation of the brain, with particular focus on Piaget's four-stage theory of cognitive development, including the key achievements at each stage and the theory's limitations.
why: Piaget's theory is one of the most influential and widely tested frameworks in developmental psychology. Understanding its stages, their defining cognitive milestones, and its limitations is directly assessed and provides a basis for evaluating experimental data about children's cognition.

items.title: I can define cognitive development and explain why it is reliant on biological maturation
items.what: Cognitive development is the continuous, lifelong development of the ability to think, comprehend, and organise information from the internal and external environment. It depends partly on the maturation of neural networks, including the frontal lobe, which is responsible for planning, decision-making, working memory, and impulse control.
items.why: Linking cognitive development to brain maturation connects this subtopic to the broader unit theme of nature-nurture interaction and explains why certain cognitive abilities cannot simply be taught before the brain is ready.
items.example: The frontal lobe does not reach full maturity until approximately age 25, which is why adolescents show greater impulsivity and less effective long-term planning than adults, even when they understand the consequences of their actions intellectually.

items.title: I can describe the four stages of Piaget's theory of cognitive development, including their age ranges and key cognitive achievements
items.what: Piaget proposed four sequential stages: Sensorimotor (0-2 years), in which infants develop object permanence and goal-directed behaviour; Preoperational (2-7 years), in which children overcome egocentrism and centration and develop reversibility; Concrete Operational (7-12 years), in which children develop conservation, classification, and simple mental operations; and Formal Operational (12+ years), in which abstract thought, logic, and reasoning emerge.
items.why: The four stages and their defining cognitive milestones are core content for this topic and are assessed both as standalone knowledge and applied to experimental scenarios.
items.example: In a conservation task, a child in the Preoperational stage (e.g. age 5) will say a rolled-out piece of clay is larger than the original ball because it looks longer, whereas a child in the Concrete Operational stage (e.g. age 9) understands the amount remains the same regardless of shape.

items.title: I can explain what object permanence and conservation are and identify at which Piagetian stages they develop
items.what: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight, and it develops in the Sensorimotor stage. Conservation is the understanding that a property of an object, such as volume or mass, remains constant even when its appearance changes, and it develops in the Concrete Operational stage.
items.why: Object permanence and conservation are the two most frequently tested Piagetian concepts in VCE Psychology data analysis questions and case studies.
items.example: A 6-month-old infant cries when a toy is covered with a cloth because, lacking object permanence, they believe the toy no longer exists. A child in the Concrete Operational stage correctly identifies that pouring water from a tall thin glass into a short wide glass does not change the total volume.

items.title: I can identify and apply the independent and dependent variables in a study testing Piaget's theory
items.what: In experiments testing Piaget's theory, the independent variable is typically the manipulation applied to the stimulus (such as the shape of clay), and the dependent variable is the children's perceptual response or judgment about the stimulus.
items.why: Identifying variables is a key science skill required across all VCE science subjects, and Piaget's conservation tasks provide a recurring context for this skill in Psychology.
items.example: In a study where 26 children are shown two equal balls of clay and one is then rolled out, the independent variable is the shape of the clay (changed by the researcher) and the dependent variable is the children's perception of whether the clay pieces are equal in size.

items.title: I can evaluate Piaget's theory by identifying at least one strength and two limitations
items.what: A strength of Piaget's theory is that each stage can be tested through simple, observable tasks such as conservation experiments. Limitations include its failure to account for developmental diversity (that development is unique to each individual), its reliance on observational data from Piaget's own children, and its rigid assignment of ages to stages that does not accommodate individual variation.
items.why: Evaluation questions requiring students to assess the adequacy of Piaget's theory are a direct exam skill at both the apply-and-analyse and evaluate levels of the VCE Psychology study design.
items.example: If Piaget's theory were fully accurate, all 26 children in a classroom of the same age should answer a conservation task identically. The fact that answers vary across the class demonstrates the theory fails to account for individual differences in the rate of cognitive development.
